notes.meaning: God says He set a trap for Babylon, and she was caught before she noticed. Many older writers link this to how the Persian king Cyrus took the city. He turned the Euphrates River aside and marched his army in along the dry riverbed at night. Babylon fell because she fought against the LORD by attacking His people, whom He guards like the apple of His eye.

God is pictured opening His armory and bringing out His weapons. Those weapons are the armies of the Medes and Persians, which He uses to carry out His anger at Babylon. "LORD of Hosts" means the commander of heaven's armies. People thought Babylon could never fall, but God has ways and means that people cannot guess.

The attackers are called from far away to break open Babylon's storehouses. When Cyrus took the city, it was full of food and riches. The proud city would be turned into heaps of ruins. God's people were always promised a remnant (a small group who survive), but Babylon is told she will have none.

The "young bulls" stand for Babylon's princes, rulers and strong soldiers. They will go down like cattle to the butcher. Their "day" is the time God has set to punish them. God has fixed times, so His people can wait patiently even when the wicked seem to be winning.

Jews who escape from Babylon will bring the news to Zion (Jerusalem) that God has paid Babylon back. This is "vengeance for His temple." Nebuchadnezzar had robbed and torn down the temple and put its holy cups in the temple of his own god. Babylon's fall would show God's people how dear they were to Him, and they should tell others about it.

God calls for archers to surround Babylon so no one gets away. The Persians were famous archers. Babylon will be treated the way she treated others, which is fair and just. Her worst sin was pride against the Holy One of Israel, not only cruelty to people. By attacking His people, she was really attacking God Himself.

Babylon's young men will fall in her own streets, not out on a battlefield. The Babylonians had hidden behind their walls after losing battles. The city was taken from the inside, and its soldiers were killed in the middle of the city.
God names Babylon "Pride" itself, as if she were the proudest of all. This points especially to the king of Babylon. God says He is against her, and her day of punishment has come.

Proud Babylon will trip and fall, and no one will help her up. Many nations served her, but none could save her when God was against her. Proud people hold their heads so high that they do not watch their steps. God will start a fire that spreads through all her cities.

God sees that both Israel and Judah are crushed under their captors, who will not let them go. He notices their slavery, just as He did in Egypt. Jeremiah first admits how hopeless things look to the exiles, so he can answer that fear in the next verse.

Their captors are strong, but their Redeemer is stronger. A "redeemer" is one who has a right to his people and buys or wins them back. God will argue their case like a lawyer in court and win it. He will bring rest to His people and trouble to Babylon. Christians have long taken comfort here too: we are weak, but our Redeemer is strong and able to keep us.

"A sword" is said again and again to show that judgment will reach everyone and everything Babylon trusted. It falls on her rulers, her wise men, her soldiers, her horses, her chariots and her riches. Her "false prophets" were fortune-tellers and star-readers who would look like fools. The "foreigners" were soldiers from other nations who served in her army. They would lose all courage.

A drought will dry up Babylon's waters. Many older writers link this to Cyrus draining the Euphrates so his army could cross. The word for her idols means "terrors," like scarecrows that only frighten children. Yet the people went wild over them. Giving God's glory to idols was a main reason for her fall.

Babylon will become a wasteland where only wild animals live. This did not happen all at once. It came step by step over hundreds of years, until only her walls were left. Prophets often speak of God's judgment in a way that looks ahead to the final end of the wicked.

Babylon will be like Sodom and Gomorrah, wiped out and empty. The same words were spoken about Edom earlier. Sodom is like a mirror showing what God's judgment on the ungodly looks like. God's own people are spared only by His mercy.

An army comes from the north: the Medes and Persians, with many allied kings from far away. They are fierce, loud like the sea, and ready as one man. These are almost the same words Jeremiah once used about Babylon's attack on Jerusalem. Now they are turned on Babylon. She is paid back in her own coin.

The king of Babylon hears the news and goes weak with fear, like a woman in labor. The Geneva Notes connect this to King Belshazzar's terror in Daniel 5. Once the people of Judah trembled at Babylon's report. Now the proud king trembles like them.

The attacker comes like a lion out of the thick bushes by the Jordan River. These words were first spoken about Edom and are now used for Babylon. That shows God deals with both by the same rule. God chooses the leader He wants for the job. No one is like God, and no "shepherd" can protect Babylon's flock from Him.

God has made His plan against Babylon, and it will not change. Like a lion dragging off weak sheep, the enemy will drag Babylon's people away. Her home will be left empty. God's words here are like a solemn promise that this will surely happen.

When Babylon falls, the whole earth shakes and the nations cry out. People thought Babylon could never be taken, so her fall amazed the world. Edom's fall was heard only as far as the Red Sea, but Babylon's fall troubles every nation.
